annotations.annotation_text: Page 330 opens Book 2, Chapter 3 ("The Tavern") during the Age of Heroes phase. This passage continues HCE behind the bar at his Chapelizod pub, the Norwegian Captain tale, the television broadcast, the twelve customers drinking and judging, featuring HCE, the Twelve Customers, Butt and Taff. The nocturnal dream-narrative layers Dublin topography, world mythology, and linguistic alchemy into polysemic prose.

annotations.annotation_text: The central conflict between Kersse and the Captain reaches its peak, illustrating the impossibility of perfectly tailoring Irishness to an outsider.
The physical deformity of the Captain ensures he cannot be easily measured or fitted, symbolizing the rugged, untamable nature of the invader.
Refusing to pay for the ruined suit, the Captain abruptly departs. This flight represents the cyclical withdrawal of the invading forces.

Mid-page polysemic node on page 330 ("The Tavern"): Joyce weaves multilingual puns across 60+ languages — etymological roots from the Contemporary Literature Press lexicons (Romanian, Scandinavian, Slavic, Classical) intersect with local Dublin speech rhythms. The Age of Heroes dream-logic transforms ordinary syntax into a palimpsest of global literary and mythic references.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind
Contemporary Literature Press: Multilingual Lexicons for FW. https://editura.mttlc.ro
Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: The economic dispute underscores the mercenary aspects of the Viking invasions and the resulting cultural debts left unpaid.
In the final cyclical iteration, the Captain returns and accepts baptism, mirroring the historical Christianization of the Norse settlements in Ireland.
The resolution of the tale shows the once-hostile foreigner becoming foundational to the new, hybridized local society.
The union with ALP's avatar permanently anchors the wandering sea-captain to the domestic, riverine landscape of Dublin.
The inevitable return of the Captain completes the Viconian ricorso, bringing the chaotic energy of the sea back into the tavern's orbit.
